entry.title: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai Awarded 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | nobelprize.org | hacker news

Discoveries in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis have earned Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Their research explains the spontaneous emergence of homochirality, the phenomenon in which chemical reactions favor one mirror-image molecular form over another.

This work resolves a century-old mystery regarding how life's molecular asymmetry originated. Such control over molecular handedness is vital for pharmaceutical manufacturing, where the specific orientation of a molecule determines its biological efficacy.

entry.title: Earth's Most Massive Species by Biomass
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | signoregalilei.com | hacker news

Domesticated cattle and Antarctic krill are the largest animal species by biomass, both surpassing the total mass of humans. In terms of total biomass, plant species such as sugar cane and boreal trees like black spruce and Dahurian larch significantly outstrip all animals.

Carbon mass measurements indicate that the carbon content of black spruce alone is nearly three times that of all animals combined. While individual organisms like the Pando aspen colony are exceptionally massive, the immense scale of boreal forest ecosystems allows tree species to dominate global biomass.

entry.title: Global Analysis Finds Ecosystem Resilience to Species Loss Is Overestimated
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | phys.org | source | hacker news

Ecosystem resilience to species loss is significantly lower than previously assumed, according to a global study in *Nature Ecology & Evolution*. Analyzing 222,829 data points across land, freshwater, and marine environments, the study found that ecosystem services—such as water purification and carbon storage—decline steadily as biodiversity decreases, rather than leveling off after a certain number of species are present.

Ocean carbon sequestration shows the strongest positive response to biodiversity, suggesting that "blue carbon" sinks depend on diverse marine communities, though researchers note this specific finding requires further study. While services like coastal flood protection may rely on specific foundational species rather than overall diversity, other benefits such as natural pest control are heavily dependent on high biodiversity levels.

entry.title: AI Agents Identify Two Room-Temperature Magnetic Semiconductor Candidates
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | vals.ai | hacker news

Research using AI agents has identified two potential Luttinger-compensated (LC) semiconductor candidates for next-generation spintronic memory. These materials are predicted to maintain zero net magnetism while allowing for spin sorting across significant energy windows at room temperature. The candidates include a newly designed compound, YBaMnFeO₅, and an existing material from 1999, KV[Cr(CN)₆].

Luttinger-compensated magnets combine the benefits of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, offering high-speed switching and high packing density without the interference of macroscopic magnetic fields. While YBaMnFeO₅ may face synthesis challenges due to its required atomic arrangement, KV[Cr(CN)₆] shows significant promise because it has already been synthesized and exhibits magnetic stability above room temperature.

This initiative represents a first in the United States, as it operates under a state regulatory agreement that allows AI technology to perform medical roles traditionally reserved for physicians.

The service is delivered via the Nolla Derm app, which uses facial scans and digital intake forms to generate automated treatment recommendations. The pilot is available to Utah residents aged 18 and older and aims to streamline access to dermatological care by reducing the need for traditional clinical consultations.

entry.title: Stephen Wolfram on the Future of Pure Math Research in the Age of AI
entry.content:
Techmeme | writings.stephenwolfram.com | hacker news

AI can effectively mine existing mathematical knowledge and facilitate connections between results, but it lacks the human imagination required to formulate the fundamental questions that drive research. A distinction is made between the statistical nature of large language models and the generative power of computation, which can produce fundamentally new results through computational irreducibility.

Human mathematical reasoning serves as a high-level sampling of a metamathematical web, allowing for the navigation of complex axiomatic systems. This process is complicated by the challenges of autoformalization, where AI may find unintended ways to satisfy formal proofs instead of accurately capturing human mathematical intent.

entry.title: Harvard's Nuclear Proximity Methodology Critiqued for Linking Proximity to Cancer Mortality
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | breakthroughjournal.org | hacker news

Authors Deric Tilson and Adam Stein argue that recent research from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health uses a flawed "proximity score" methodology that incorrectly links living near nuclear power plants to increased cancer mortality. Replicating the analysis shows that the approach assigns cancer risks to various landmarks, including Costco warehouses and major league sports venues, based on geographic proximity rather than actual radiation exposure.

The methodology fails to distinguish between geographic proximity and actual radiation dose, noting that most residents near nuclear facilities receive no measurable radiation. Such approaches capture statistical noise and create false correlations, potentially leading to misguided public health narratives and policies.

entry.title: Loss of Cell Identity Model Proposed as Driver of Aging
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | erictopol.substack.com | hacker news

New research in Nature and Cell proposes that human aging is driven by the loss of cellular identity rather than solely by cumulative molecular damage. This process, known as "decanalization," involves the erosion of the epigenetic structures—specifically the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)—that maintain a cell's specialized functional state. This instability leads to "mesenchymal drift," a process where cells transition into a fibroblast-like state, contributing to systemic inflammation and fibrous scarring.

This cellular drift is linked to the progression of age-related diseases, such as Alzheimer’s and atherosclerosis. Potential interventions to mitigate or reverse this process include partial epigenetic reprogramming via Yamanaka factors, the use of lithium to preserve neuronal identity, and the metabolic regulation of epigenetic architecture through caloric restriction.
